label: UMP unbiased and UMP invariant tests — mastery test (unseen)

items.stem: For a one-parameter exponential family and the alternative H₁: θ ≠ θ₀, a UMP test of size α:
items.explanation: The most powerful region against an alternative above θ₀ and the one against an alternative below θ₀ are disjoint tails of the same distribution, so no single region can be most powerful against every alternative. The two-tailed region is a valid size-α test but is not UMP, which is the distinction June 2026 Q14 was built on.

items.stem: The Neyman–Pearson lemma applies to:
options: a composite null against a composite alternative
a simple null against a composite alternative
a simple null against a simple alternative
items.explanation: The lemma requires both hypotheses to be completely specified. Composite alternatives need monotone likelihood ratio and Karlin–Rubin, and even then only when the alternative is one-sided.

items.stem: A test is called unbiased if:
options: its power equals its size at every alternative
the statistic it uses is an unbiased estimator
its power is at least its size at every alternative
its size equals the stated level exactly
items.explanation: An unbiased test satisfies π(θ) ≥ α for every θ in the alternative — it is never worse than ignoring the data. The term has nothing to do with unbiased estimation, which is a different idea sharing a word.

items.stem: For the density f(x; θ) = θe^(−θx) and H₀: θ = θ₀ against H₁: θ > θ₀, the UMP test rejects for:
items.explanation: Here θ is the rate, so the mean is 1/θ and a larger θ produces smaller observations. The likelihood ratio L(θ₂)/L(θ₁) for θ₂ > θ₁ decreases in Σxᵢ, so Karlin–Rubin places the critical region in the lower tail. Reading θ as the mean reverses this and is the commonest error in the topic.

items.stem: Arrange the steps of deciding what kind of optimal test is available in the correct order.
items.explanation: Check the sidedness of the alternative first, because that alone decides whether a UMP test can exist. If it is one-sided, verify MLR and apply Karlin–Rubin. If it is two-sided, there is no UMP test and the question becomes which restricted class to optimise within.
items: A. If one-sided, check monotone likelihood ratio and apply Karlin–Rubin
B. If two-sided, conclude that no UMP test exists among all tests
C. Determine whether the alternative is one-sided or two-sided
D. Restrict to unbiased or invariant tests and find the best one there

items.stem: For an iid sample of size n = 8 from f(x; θ) = θe^(−θx), the quantity 2θΣxᵢ has a chi-square distribution with how many degrees of freedom?
items.explanation: Each 2θXᵢ is exponential with mean 2, which is a chi-square with 2 degrees of freedom, and n independent ones add to 2n = 16. The factor 2 in front of the sum and the doubling of the degrees of freedom go together. June 2026 Q14 wrote χ²(α, n) in its preamble but used 2n inside its options, so read the options rather than the preamble.
items.check: The degrees of freedom are 2n, so they must be even and twice the sample size. An answer equal to n, or to n − 1, has dropped the doubling.

items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be iid with f(x; θ) = θe^(−θx). For testing H₀: θ = θ₀ against H₁: θ ≠ θ₀, the UMP critical region of size α is:
items.explanation: This is June 2026 Q14. The alternative is two-sided, and the most powerful regions against the two sides are disjoint, so no UMP test exists. The first option is the UMP region for the one-sided H₁: θ > θ₀ and was the most-marked wrong answer; the second is the region for θ < θ₀; the third is the two-tailed test, which is valid and useful but not UMP.

items.stem: X₁,…,X₅ are iid with f(x; θ) = θe^(−θx). For H₀: θ = 1 against H₁: θ > 1 at α = 0.05, with χ²(0.95, 10) = 3.9403 and χ²(0.05, 10) = 18.3070, the UMP test rejects when Σxᵢ is:
items.explanation: Against θ > 1 the region is the lower tail, so the cut-off is the lower 5% point of the chi-square with 10 df — which is its upper 95% point, 3.9403 — divided by 2θ₀ = 2, giving 1.9701. Option A is the region for θ < 1. The remaining options omit the division by 2θ₀.
items.check: Two conversions must both happen: the lower α point is the upper (1 − α) point, and the chi-square value is divided by 2θ₀. Missing the division leaves a number twice too large.

items.stem: A one-sided test built for H₁: θ > θ₀ is applied when the true alternative is two-sided. At alternatives below θ₀ its power is:
items.explanation: The rejection region sits in the tail where alternatives below θ₀ make the data LESS likely than the null does, so the chance of landing in it falls below α. For n = 5, θ₀ = 1 and α = 0.05 the power at θ = 0.5 is 0.003. Power below size is the definition of a biased test — the test is misleading, not merely weak.

items.stem: For H₀: μ = μ₀ against H₁: μ ≠ μ₀ in N(μ, σ²) with σ² known, the two-sided z test is:
items.explanation: It is not UMP — no test is, because the alternative is two-sided and the non-existence argument applies to the normal family as much as to any other. But its power function has its minimum at μ₀, so it is unbiased, and among unbiased tests it is most powerful. UMPU is the precise sense in which this familiar test is optimal.

items.stem: Consider testing H₀: θ = θ₀ against the two-sided alternative H₁: θ ≠ θ₀ in a one-parameter exponential family.
items.explanation: A is true, and it is the reason for the non-existence. B is false — the two-tailed region is a perfectly valid size-α test, it merely is not UMP. C is true: the one-sided test's power drops below α on the far side. D is false; a UMPU test does exist for this problem and is two-tailed, which is the whole point of the unbiasedness restriction.
statements: The most powerful regions against alternatives above and below θ₀ are disjoint.
The two-tailed region is not a valid test of size α.
A one-sided test applied here is biased, with power below α on one side.
No optimal test of any kind exists for this problem.

A.why: True. One is a lower tail of the sufficient statistic and the other an upper tail, with no outcome in common — which is exactly why no single region can win against both.

B.why: False. The two-tailed region has size α and is the test one would actually use. It simply is not uniformly most powerful among all tests.

C.why: True. Its power falls below α at alternatives on the far side — 0.003 against a size of 0.05 in the standard worked case.

D.why: False. Restricting to unbiased tests yields a UMPU test, and restricting to invariant tests yields a UMP invariant test. Optimality is available; it is just relative to a class.

items.stem: The cut-offs of a two-sided UMPU test are determined by:
options: the size condition alone, split equally between the tails
the size condition together with E[φ(T)T | θ₀] = α E[T | θ₀]
the size condition together with the requirement that the test be invariant
maximising the power at a single chosen alternative
items.explanation: Two unknown cut-offs need two equations. The second one is the unbiasedness condition, and it is equivalent to requiring the power function to have its minimum exactly at θ₀. Splitting α equally satisfies the size condition only, and in general fails the second.

items.stem: The equal-tail two-sided test, with α/2 in each tail, is UMP unbiased:
options: only when the null distribution of the statistic is symmetric
items.explanation: Equal tails always gives the right size, but it satisfies the unbiasedness condition only when symmetry makes the power minimum fall at θ₀. That holds for the normal mean, so the two-sided z test is UMPU. It fails for a skewed law such as the chi-square of an exponential sum, where the UMPU cut-offs are unequal.

items.stem: For H₀: μ = 0 against H₁: μ ≠ 0 in N(μ, σ²) with σ² unknown, the two-sided t test is UMP invariant under the group of:
options: scale changes xᵢ → cxᵢ with c > 0
all one-to-one transformations of the data
items.explanation: Multiplying every observation by a positive constant sends μ to cμ and σ to cσ, so μ = 0 if and only if cμ = 0 and the problem maps onto itself. The t statistic is unchanged by that transformation and is the maximal invariant. A location shift would move μ away from 0 and change the hypothesis, so it is not a symmetry of this problem.

items.stem: X₁,…,X₅ are iid with f(x; θ) = θe^(−θx). For H₀: θ = 1 against H₁: θ < 1 at α = 0.05, with χ²(0.05, 10) = 18.3070, the UMP test rejects when Σxᵢ is:
items.explanation: A smaller rate means larger observations, so the region against θ < 1 is the upper tail: 2Σxᵢ ≥ 18.3070, giving Σxᵢ ≥ 9.1535. Option A is the region for the opposite alternative, option C omits the division by 2θ₀, and option D has the inequality reversed.
items.check: Smaller rate, larger sum, upper tail. The chi-square point is divided by 2θ₀ = 2, and the inequality points the same way as the tail.

items.stem: Which statement about the hierarchy of optimality notions is correct?
options: UMP is a weaker requirement than UMP unbiased
A UMPU test is most powerful among all size-α tests
UMP requires one test to be most powerful at every alternative, while UMPU requires this only among unbiased tests
UMP invariant and UMPU are two names for the same property
items.explanation: UMP is the stronger demand, made over all size-α tests; UMPU narrows the competition to unbiased tests, which is why a winner exists two-sided. A UMPU test can be beaten at a particular alternative by a biased test, so the second option is false. UMPU and UMP invariant are different restrictions that happen to pick out the same test for the standard normal problems.

items.stem: Consider the equal-tail two-sided test for the exponential rate parameter, with n = 5, θ₀ = 1 and α = 0.05, based on 2Σxᵢ being chi-square with 10 degrees of freedom.
items.explanation: A is true — the cut-offs 3.2470 and 20.4832 are the 0.975 and 0.025 points of the 10-degree-of-freedom law, and the two tails sum to exactly 0.05. B is false: evaluated with 2n + 2 = 12 degrees of freedom the unbiasedness condition comes out as 0.0649, not 0.0500, so the test is not UMPU. C is true, and it is why the equal-tail test remains standard practice. D is false — a UMPU test does exist here; its cut-offs are simply unequal.
statements: The equal-tail test has size exactly 0.05.
The equal-tail test satisfies the unbiasedness condition and is therefore UMPU.
The equal-tail test is a valid test and is the one used in practice.
Because equal tails fails the unbiasedness condition, no UMPU test exists for this problem.

A.why: True. The cut-offs are the 0.975 and 0.025 points of the chi-square with 10 df, so the two tail probabilities are 0.025 each.

B.why: False. The unbiasedness condition evaluates the same tail probabilities with two extra degrees of freedom, giving 0.0649 against the required 0.0500. The power minimum is therefore not at θ₀.

C.why: True. The loss of power is small and the equal-tail cut-offs are far easier to tabulate, so this is a deliberate and accepted approximation in applied work.

D.why: False. The UMPU test exists and is found by solving the size and unbiasedness conditions together; the solution simply has unequal tail areas.

items.stem: For the one-sided UMP test of H₀: θ = 1 against H₁: θ > 1 for an exponential rate with n = 5 and α = 0.05, rejecting when Σxᵢ ≤ 1.9701, the power at θ = 0.5 is approximately:
items.explanation: Under θ = 0.5 the quantity 2(0.5)Σxᵢ = Σxᵢ is chi-square with 10 df, so the power is P(χ²₁₀ ≤ 1.9701) = 0.003. That is far below the size of 0.05, which is the precise sense in which the test is biased at alternatives on the far side. Option C is the power at θ = 2, on the side the test was built for.
items.check: Power below the size of 0.05 is the expected answer here — that is what biased means. A value above 0.05 means the power was evaluated on the wrong side of θ₀.

items.stem: A test is UMPU of size α. Which of the following is possible?
options: It is also the most powerful test against every simple alternative
Another size-α test has greater power at every alternative
Its power is below α at some alternative
Another size-α test has greater power at some alternative
items.explanation: A UMPU test is best only within the unbiased class, so a BIASED size-α test can beat it at a particular alternative — the one-sided test does exactly that on its own side. It cannot be beaten everywhere at once by a size-α test, its power cannot fall below α since it is unbiased, and it cannot be most powerful against every simple alternative, because such a test would be UMP and none exists two-sided.

items.stem: The two-sided t test for a normal mean with σ² unknown is both UMP invariant and UMPU. What does this coincidence indicate?
options: that UMP invariance and unbiasedness are equivalent requirements
that two different restrictions happen to select the same test for this problem
that the t test is UMP among all size-α tests
that the t test has no optimality property at all
items.explanation: Invariance under scale changes and unbiasedness are different principles, and in general they could select different tests. For the standard normal problems they agree, which is a large part of why those tests feel inevitable — but it is a feature of the normal family, not a theorem about the two notions. The t test is still not UMP, because the alternative is two-sided.
